false_negatives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Serialize index creation per key before publishing to the cache

The narrowed cache lock allows GetIndex to return nil while an index for that same key is being built. Concurrent searches, or a search and the write-event handler, can therefore build separate indexes for one NamespacedResource. If the event handler publishes its index and applies an update before the other builder publishes, the latter replaces the updated index with its older snapshot, losing the update from search results. Disk-backed builds can also compete to create the same directory and fail. Keep builds for different keys parallel, but coordinate creation for the same key and recheck the cache before building.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Retain the stopped-state check when removing lazy initialization

Removing the Init checks also removes the request guard against shutdown: Stop sets initErr to 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped', and previously subsequent calls to Init returned that error without executing the operation. Create, Update, Delete and the other RPCs now continue accessing the backend after Stop. For the SQL backend, Stop only cancels polling and does not disable database writes, so requests can successfully mutate resources after the watchers have stopped. Replace the lazy-init checks with an explicit lifecycle-state guard rather than removing the shutdown protection.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Register cleanup for the actual created provider aliases

The new test creates providers named idp-alias-0 through idp-alias-19 but registers every cleanup against the literal provider name "alias"; the same mistake occurs for idp-alias-20 at line 425. Cleanup therefore attempts to delete a nonexistent provider instead of the created resources, potentially failing teardown and leaving realm-level providers behind to contaminate later tests. false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Use persisted enabled state when deciding login-cache invalidation

The original model passed to this method comes from getById(), which wraps isEnabled() to return false when its organization (or organization support in the realm) is disabled. The login query, however, caches IDs based on the persisted IDP fields. For example, populate the cache for a public enabled organization IDP, disable its organization, then set hideOnLogin=true on the IDP. Both predicates here return false, so the cached membership is retained. After re-enabling the organization, getForLogin still returns that hidden IDP, and OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only rechecks isEnabled(), so it displays the provider despite hideOnLogin. Compare unwrapped persisted models for invalidation rather than organization-dependent enabled state.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)

Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations

false_positives.candidate:
Exercise the actual ES384 and ES512 curves and verify the reconstructed signature

All three tests generate an EC key using the provider's default curve (normally P-256), including testES384 and testES512. Changing the hash algorithm does not change the curve, so these tests only pad P-256 integers to larger lengths and never exercise real P-384 or P-521 signatures, including the long-form DER sequence length needed for P-521. Moreover, comparing two concatenated conversions can pass when the first conversion loses data. Generate the appropriate curve for each algorithm and verify the reconstructed DER signature against the original data and public key.

Reject concatenated signatures with an unexpected length

concatenatedRSToASN1DER copies only the first signLength bytes without checking signature.length. An otherwise valid JOSE ECDSA signature with arbitrary bytes appended therefore produces exactly the same DER signature and can still verify successfully. JOSE requires the exact fixed signature length; accepting these inputs permits token/signature malleability. Check the input length and throw IOException before copying (also avoiding unchecked array-copy exceptions for short inputs).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

Global view permission bypasses client-specific denials

canView(ClientModel) returns true as soon as canView() grants the all-clients VIEW permission, without evaluating permissions on the requested client. Consequently, an administrator granted VIEW on all clients can still read a client for which a client-specific VIEW permission explicitly denies access. true_positives.matched_candidate:
View-only group permission allows top-level group creation

canManage() accepts either the VIEW or MANAGE scope on all groups. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() calls requireManage(), which delegates to this method, so an administrator granted only read access can create groups or move an existing subgroup to the top level. true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorization resource IDs are used as group model IDs

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission() and returns it as a group ID. Authorization resources are created with generated IDs; the corresponding GroupModel ID is stored in the resource name by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource(). Consequently the permission lookup misses the specific resource and falls back to all-groups permissions, and the returned IDs cannot match user group memberships when UsersResource applies the search filter. When creating an individual group authorization resource, getOrCreateResource() sets its name and scopes but never sets its type to Groups. This resource uses i18next-style double-brace placeholders, but the new message replaces them with Java MessageFormat placeholders and a choice expression. Validate HTML inside choice branches rather than discarding it

A translation such as {0,choice,0#<script>alert(1)</script>|1#value} therefore passes verification because the executable markup is replaced with '...'. false_positives.candidate:
Global view permission bypasses client-specific denials

canView(ClientModel) returns true as soon as canView() grants the all-clients VIEW permission, without evaluating permissions on the requested client. Consequently, an administrator granted VIEW on all clients can still read a client for which a client-specific VIEW permission explicitly denies access. This defeats the resource-specific override behavior used by V2 permissions (and tested for users in UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest). Keep the built-in admin-role shortcut, but evaluate fine-grained view access through the client-specific resource, falling back to the all-clients resource only when appropriate.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorization resource IDs are used as group model IDs

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission() and returns it as a group ID. Authorization resources are created with generated IDs; the corresponding GroupModel ID is stored in the resource name by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource(). Consequently the permission lookup misses the specific resource and falls back to all-groups permissions, and the returned IDs cannot match user group memberships when UsersResource applies the search filter. Use the mapped group model ID rather than the authorization resource ID, and handle the all-groups resource separately.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug in `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()`: `groupResource.getId()` (the authorization resource ID) is mistakenly passed to `hasPermission()` and returned as a group ID, whereas the actual group ID is stored in the resource name. false_positives.candidate:
Individual group resources are not assigned the Groups type

When creating an individual group authorization resource, getOrCreateResource() sets its name and scopes but never sets its type to Groups. The new GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() discovers resources exclusively through findByType(..., "Groups", ...), so individual group permissions are omitted from that discovery. This prevents group-member permissions from supplying the group filters needed by user searches and counts. Assign the resource type when creating the resource and test discovery of an individual group's member-view permission.

Reject concatenated signatures with an unexpected length

concatenatedRSToASN1DER copies only the first signLength bytes without checking signature.length. An otherwise valid JOSE ECDSA signature with arbitrary bytes appended therefore produces exactly the same DER signature and can still verify successfully. JOSE requires the exact fixed signature length; accepting these inputs permits token/signature malleability. Check the input length and throw IOException before copying (also avoiding unchecked array-copy exceptions for short inputs).

Exercise the actual ES384 and ES512 curves and verify the reconstructed signature

All three tests generate an EC key using the provider's default curve (normally P-256), including testES384 and testES512. Changing the hash algorithm does not change the curve, so these tests only pad P-256 integers to larger lengths and never exercise real P-384 or P-521 signatures, including the long-form DER sequence length needed for P-521. Moreover, comparing two concatenated conversions can pass when the first conversion loses data. Generate the appropriate curve for each algorithm and verify the reconstructed DER signature against the original data and public key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Spawned workers do not pass the multiprocessing.Process type check

Workers are created with multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process, which creates SpawnProcess instances. These are not instances of the top-level multiprocessing.Process class, so this check skips kill() for every production worker. When a worker hangs, the manager starts a replacement without stopping the original; the original can subsequently resume flushing the same shards, causing concurrent processing and duplicate production. The identical check in join() also skips termination. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or explicitly distinguish threads from the spawn-context process type.

Even after correcting the process type check, this early break still leaks workers. The deadline should limit waiting, not skip termination of the remaining processes.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Serialize index creation per key before publishing to the cache

The narrowed cache lock allows GetIndex to return nil while an index for that same key is being built. Concurrent searches, or a search and the write-event handler, can therefore build separate indexes for one NamespacedResource. If the event handler publishes its index and applies an update before the other builder publishes, the latter replaces the updated index with its older snapshot, losing the update from search results. Disk-backed builds can also compete to create the same directory and fail. Keep builds for different keys parallel, but coordinate creation for the same key and recheck the cache before building.

For the SQL backend, Stop only cancels polling and does not disable database writes, so requests can successfully mutate resources after the watchers have stopped. Replace the lazy-init checks with an explicit lifecycle-state guard rather than removing the shutdown protection.

false_positives.candidate:
Create a fresh queue pool for each partition assignment

The factory creates its queue pool only once and passes that same pool to every strategy. Closing or joining a strategy shuts down that pool's workers and queues, but a Kafka rebalance subsequently calls create_with_partitions on the same factory and receives another strategy backed by the stopped pool. New messages then either accumulate without workers or fail to enqueue and are marked completed by submit's exception handler, allowing unprocessed results to be committed. Bound queued work and apply backpressure

Each work queue is created with no maximum size, and submit always accepts more messages without raising MessageRejected. If processing is slower than Kafka ingestion, or a worker stalls, the consumer continues retaining decoded results and original messages indefinitely. The offset tracker also retains all later offsets behind unfinished work. This can exhaust consumer memory under exactly the slow-item workload this mode is intended to handle; queued and in-flight work need a bound with backpressure.

Drain accepted work before stopping workers and committing final offsets

Graceful shutdown sets every worker's shutdown flag before shutting down the queues. Workers therefore exit after their current item instead of draining queued items, despite shutdown(immediate=False). In addition, strategy.close stops the commit thread before waiting for workers, so results completed during shutdown never receive a final commit. Normal shutdown or partition revocation abandons accepted work and replays already processed results on the next assignment. close/join should drain accepted work (within the supplied timeout) and commit its completed offsets before stopping.

Track delivered offset order rather than requiring consecutive Kafka offsets

The tracker stops at any integer offset absent from all_offsets, even if every delivered message has completed. Kafka can legitimately deliver nonconsecutive offsets, for example when transactional control records or aborted transactions are skipped. If completed offsets 100 and 102 are present in the same commit scan, it commits only 100 even though 102 is safe; with ongoing work after such gaps this unnecessarily retains completed offsets and increases replay and memory usage. Determine the safe prefix of delivered offsets, stopping at outstanding work rather than at offsets Kafka never delivered.

false_positives.candidate:
Create a fresh queue pool for each partition assignment

The factory creates its queue pool only once and passes that same pool to every strategy. Closing or joining a strategy shuts down that pool's workers and queues, but a Kafka rebalance subsequently calls create_with_partitions on the same factory and receives another strategy backed by the stopped pool. New messages then either accumulate without workers or fail to enqueue and are marked completed by submit's exception handler, allowing unprocessed results to be committed. Bound queued work and apply backpressure

Each work queue is created with no maximum size, and submit always accepts more messages without raising MessageRejected. If processing is slower than Kafka ingestion, or a worker stalls, the consumer continues retaining decoded results and original messages indefinitely. The offset tracker also retains all later offsets behind unfinished work. This can exhaust consumer memory under exactly the slow-item workload this mode is intended to handle; queued and in-flight work need a bound with backpressure.

Drain accepted work before stopping workers and committing final offsets

Graceful shutdown sets every worker's shutdown flag before shutting down the queues. Workers therefore exit after their current item instead of draining queued items, despite shutdown(immediate=False). In addition, strategy.close stops the commit thread before waiting for workers, so results completed during shutdown never receive a final commit. Normal shutdown or partition revocation abandons accepted work and replays already processed results on the next assignment. close/join should drain accepted work (within the supplied timeout) and commit its completed offsets before stopping.

The tracker stops at any integer offset absent from all_offsets, even if every delivered message has completed. If completed offsets 100 and 102 are present in the same commit scan, it commits only 100 even though 102 is safe; with ongoing work after such gaps this unnecessarily retains completed offsets and increases replay and memory usage. true_positives.golden_comment: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Exact multiples of the page size produce an empty extra page

totalPages uses floor(user_count / limit) + 1, so a group with 50 members and a limit of 50 reports two pages. The Next action remains enabled on the actual last page and requests offset 50, displaying an empty member list. Use ceiling division for nonempty groups so the page count and showingLast match the available results.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug. The totalPages formula floor(user_count/limit)+1 adds an extra empty page when user_count is an exact multiple of limit. Both suggest ceiling division as the fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Public member lists are truncated without a way to load subsequent pages

The shared findMembers method now requests only 50 members, and the server applies that limit to all groups. This public route fetches only once, while the public group/members template has no pagination or load-more controls. Consequently, members beyond the first 50 are inaccessible on the public group page; previously nonautomatic groups returned their complete membership. Add pagination to the public page alongside the new paginated response.

Existing membership PATCH requests silently hide groups

The resources route still accepts PATCH /admin/groups/:id, but update no longer handles the previously supported changes: {add: ... , delete: ...} payload. Such a request now ignores the membership changes and sets visible to false because it contains no visible parameter, then returns success. Existing API clients therefore silently lose their membership updates and unintentionally hide the group. Preserve the PATCH contract or explicitly reject unsupported payloads without modifying the group.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent matches lose counter increments

The match counter is updated using a read-modify-save sequence without locking. Two simultaneous checks for the same blocked email can both read the same match_count and save the same incremented value, recording only one match instead of two. Use an atomic database increment or a locked update to preserve the statistics under concurrent registration attempts.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment flags side effects in a predicate method, and it names race conditions under concurrency as one consequence. The candidate covers that race-condition part: non-atomic match_count updates in the same method. It does not raise the misleading naming or the side-effect concern itself. Because the race condition is explicitly part of the golden comment and both point at the same code (the stats update inside should_block_email?), this is likely a partial match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Case-sensitive lookup allows blocked addresses to register

BlockedEmail looks up the supplied email with an exact, case-sensitive equality comparison, and neither this model nor User.new_from_params normalizes it. A block for `block@example.com` therefore does not stop registration with `block@EXAMPLE.COM`, even though the domain refers to the same mailbox. Normalize addresses consistently when storing blocked entries and checking user emails so casing cannot bypass the block.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the case-sensitive email lookup in BlockedEmail, which lets a differently cased address get past the block. That is the same issue.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Apply the website visibility restriction to website_name

The new website_name attribute is not included in untrusted_attributes, and include_website_name lacks the trailing '?' required for a serializer inclusion predicate. Consequently, an anonymous viewer of a TL0 user receives the website hostname (and, for matching domains, its path) even when scope.restrict_user_fields? suppresses website. The template also displays this leaked value because it now checks website_name independently. Apply the same restriction as website and add a test with a populated TL0 website.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly notes that include_website_name lacks the trailing '?' needed for a serializer inclusion predicate, which is the golden comment's main point. It also adds a related security consequence. This is the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed imports persist unsanitized HTML as cooked posts

Imported contents are parsed by Nokogiri but never sanitized before being saved with the raw_html cook method, which returns the HTML unchanged. PollFeed passes feed content directly into this method, so script tags, event-handler attributes, and dangerous links from a feed become stored executable content on the forum's origin. The source URL is also interpolated into HTML without escaping. Sanitize the final imported HTML, including the attribution link, before bypassing the cooking pipeline.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment raises two issues: a nil-contents NoMethodError and XSS from the unescaped url interpolation. The candidate explicitly says the source URL is interpolated into HTML without escaping, which covers the XSS part. It does not mention the nil issue, but it partially matches the same underlying concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid Ruby prevents the discussion template from rendering

The conditional is closed with `end if` rather than `end`. The trailing `if` has no condition, so the generated ERB Ruby fails to compile. Every embed request that finds an existing topic will fail instead of displaying the discussion. Close the block with `end` and add a test that renders the actual view.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the ERB block closed with 'end if' instead of 'end', which is invalid Ruby and breaks rendering. The fix in both is to use 'end'.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
RSS entries without a content element abort feed polling

The poller unconditionally calls `scrub` on `i.content`. Valid RSS feeds commonly provide article text in `description` rather than a content element; for those entries, content is nil and polling raises instead of importing the entry. Since the exception exits the loop and retries are disabled, later entries also go unprocessed. Handle missing content and use the appropriate RSS description fallback.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: `scrub` is called unconditionally on `i.content`, which is nil for RSS entries that lack a content element, so it crashes. Both also propose falling back to `description`.

false_positives.candidate:
Relative URL conversion corrupts protocol-relative links

The URL conversion treats every href beginning with `/` as a path on the article host. A valid protocol-relative link such as `//cdn.example.com/file` is consequently rewritten to `http://article-host/cdn.example.com/file`; the image conversion below has the same problem. Path-relative links such as `images/photo.jpg` are not resolved at all and instead point at the forum when rendered there. Resolve references against the full source URI rather than concatenating the source host.

Remote retrieval follows redirects outside the allowed embed host

TopicRetriever validates only the initial URL's host, then this method fetches it with open-uri, which follows HTTP redirects. An allowed-host URL that redirects to another host can therefore cause the worker to fetch internal HTTP services and publish their extracted content as a topic, bypassing the embedding host restriction. Validate redirect destinations and resolved addresses before each request, rejecting private or otherwise disallowed targets.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The second downsize definition replaces the existing API

Ruby does not overload methods by argument signature: this definition replaces the preceding `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` method. Existing callers supplying width, height, and options will now raise ArgumentError. Callers supplying only width and height will bind the height to `opts`, then fail when optimization accesses `opts[:allow_animation]`. Preserve both calling conventions in a single method or give the dimensions-string variant a separate name.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same issue: a duplicate downsize definition overrides the original width/height signature, which breaks existing callers.

false_positives.candidate:
Large animated GIFs lose their animation even when it is allowed

The new downsizing call passes the upload's temporary path rather than its original filename. `OptimizedImage.optimize` selects animated processing only when the source path ends in `.gif`, but multipart upload tempfiles normally have no such extension. Consequently, even with `allow_animated_thumbnails` enabled, a large animated GIF is processed by the static ImageMagick instructions, which read only frame `[0]`. Because this operation overwrites the upload itself, the animation is permanently discarded before storage. Detect the image format independently of the tempfile extension or use a correctly suffixed temporary file.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes when the current user has no TopicUser record

TopicUser.find_by can return nil for a visible topic the current user has never visited. This can happen when an email link is opened while logged into a different account or when a forwarded link is opened. The action then dereferences tu.notification_level and returns a server error instead of handling the unsubscribe. Resolve the default notification level and create the user's preference record when none exists.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: TopicUser.find_by returns nil when no record exists, and the code then calls methods on tu, causing a crash.

false_positives.candidate:
Notification preferences are mutated by an unprotected GET request

The new GET unsubscribe route immediately saves notification preferences for the session's current user, without a recipient token or a POST confirmation. Rails CSRF protection does not protect GET requests, so another site can navigate a logged-in user to this URL and silently downgrade or mute notifications for a topic. Keep GET read-only and perform the change through a CSRF-protected request (or an appropriately validated recipient-specific unsubscribe token).

Direct save allows automatic tracking to undo unsubscribe

The unsubscribe action updates notification_level directly and saves the TopicUser without setting notifications_reason_id. For users whose topic tracking was automatic and whose reason is still nil, TopicUser.update_last_read explicitly restores tracking once the reading-time threshold is exceeded. Consequently, reading the topic after unsubscribing can undo this explicit preference. Use TopicUser.change, as set_notifications does, so the user_changed reason and notification-change metadata are recorded.

Client-side entry never performs the unsubscribe operation

The Ember unsubscribe route only loads the ordinary topic view through PostStream.loadTopicView; it never calls the unsubscribe endpoint or changes the notification level. When this URL is entered through client-side navigation, the Rails HTML GET action does not run, yet the template tells the user they will stop receiving notifications. Ensure this flow explicitly performs the preference change rather than relying on an initial full-page server request.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

false_positives.candidate:
Invalidate connected calendar queries after deleting cache

The cache deletion success handler only invokes the optional onSuccess callback and never invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars. The wrapper displaying cacheUpdatedAt owns that query but merely forwards props.onChanged, which is optional and does not guarantee a refetch; it also disables refetchOnWindowFocus. Consequently, after a successful deletion the dropdown can continue showing the old cache timestamp and offering deletion of data that no longer exists. Invalidate the connected calendar queries on successful cache deletion, as the disconnect mutation already does.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

false_positives.candidate:
Date overrides bypass calendar and booking conflict checks

When an override exists on the slot's date, checkIfIsAvailable returns true before evaluating busy times. An override defines working availability, not permission to ignore existing bookings or external calendar events. Consequently, personal events and fixed or round-robin hosts with an override can expose slots that overlap their existing bookings. Continue to the busy-time checks after validating the override.

Override validation checks overlap instead of full slot containment

The new override checks reject only slots ending at or before the override start or starting after its end. For a fixed host available from 10:00 to 11:00, a round-robin slot from 09:30 to 10:30 or 10:30 to 11:30 therefore passes, even though the host is unavailable for part of the meeting. A slot starting exactly at 11:00 also passes. Require the entire slot to fit within an override interval.

Multiple override intervals reject slots inside a valid interval

dateOverrides.find searches for any interval that excludes the slot, rather than an interval that contains it. If a host has overrides of 09:00–12:00 and 14:00–17:00 on the same date, a 10:00 slot is rejected by the afternoon interval and a 15:00 slot by the morning interval. Split date-override availability can therefore lose all its slots. Group overrides by date and accept containment in any of that date's intervals.

Working-hours validation rejects ordinary split schedules

The workingHours.find predicate rejects a slot if it is outside any working-hours interval on that weekday. For a normal schedule of 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, morning slots fail against the afternoon interval and afternoon slots fail against the morning interval. Because every host now goes through this check, this removes valid slots even on dates without overrides. Validate that the full slot is contained in at least one applicable interval instead.

Timezone conversion discards midnight rollover

The converted override boundaries retain only hour and minute, discarding their date. For example, a UTC override from 22:00 to 23:00 viewed in UTC+01:30 becomes startTime 1410 and endTime 30. buildSlots discards that range because start is greater than end, so the valid 23:30–00:30 availability disappears. Converted overrides that cross an attendee's midnight need to be split across the corresponding attendee dates rather than reduced to a single minute-of-day range.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Increment retryCount atomically instead of writing a stale value

Both failure paths set retryCount to the value fetched at the beginning of the cron run plus one. If two cron requests overlap and both fail to schedule the same reminder, they read the same count and overwrite each other, so two failures are recorded as only one. This allows reminders to exceed the intended two-failure limit. Use Prisma's atomic increment operation in both failure paths.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: retryCount is set from a stale value plus one, so concurrent runs can lose increments. Both recommend Prisma's atomic increment, and both say the fix applies to both failure paths.

false_positives.candidate:
Do not let failure bookkeeping abort the remaining reminder batch

The new workflowReminder.update inside the catch block can itself throw and is not protected. For example, if a reminder is deleted after findMany (by a concurrent cleanup run or workflow deletion), scheduling or the success update can fail, and this catch then attempts to update a nonexistent row. Prisma throws, terminating the handler and leaving every remaining reminder in the batch unprocessed. Previously the catch logged the error and continued. Make the retry update tolerate deleted rows and preserve per-reminder error isolation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

false_positives.candidate:
Preserve or migrate the removed findMany API

The exported InsightsBookingService no longer exposes findMany; it now only returns SQL fragments through getBaseConditions. Existing callers of findMany will fail type checking (or throw at runtime), and callers using the previous WhereInput-returning condition methods cannot pass the new Sql objects to Prisma model queries. This PR updates only the integration test, not production consumers. Migrate all consumers to parameterized $queryRaw queries in the same change, or retain a compatible querying API until that migration is complete.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Do not replace omitted refresh tokens with a placeholder

This helper injects the literal string "refresh_token" whenever a response omits a refresh token, including when credential sharing is disabled. Office365 explicitly allows refresh_token to be omitted and merges the parsed response into the existing credentials, so this now overwrites the real stored refresh token with an unusable placeholder. The following refresh fails and the user must reconnect. Preserve the existing token when the provider does not return a replacement.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: when the refresh_token is missing, it gets set to the literal string 'refresh_token'. That replaces the real token, so later refreshes fail and authentication breaks.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Computed Zod keys do not validate or preserve expiry fields

Calling toString() on a Zod schema produces a literal property name (normally "[object Object]"), not a wildcard for response properties. Both computed keys therefore collide, and this z.object also strips unrecognized properties such as expires_in, expiry_date and refresh_token. With credential sharing enabled, valid refresh responses lose their expiry and refresh token; Zoom then computes a NaN expiry and other integrations cannot persist usable refreshed credentials. Use explicit supported fields or a passthrough schema with appropriate validation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same problem: the computed [z.string().toString()] keys in minimumTokenResponseSchema are invalid or broken Zod usage. The golden comment says this throws a runtime error, while the candidate says it produces wrong behavior by stripping fields. The predicted consequences differ, but the bug location and root cause are the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Persist parsed Google credentials rather than the safeParse result

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the safeParse result envelope, { success: true, data: ... }, whereas the previous schema.parse returned the credential object itself. Writing this result directly to credential.key stores the envelope instead of access_token, refresh_token and expiry_date at the top level. The next GoogleCalendarService construction fails googleCredentialSchema.parse, breaking calendar access after a refresh even with syncing disabled. Store the result's data.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the safeParse envelope, and that envelope is stored as credential.key instead of the parsed token data. Both propose the same fix, storing .data.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Normalize sync responses to the contracts expected by SDK callers

The sync branch returns a native fetch Response, but several callers still expect the result of their original refresh function: Google and both Zoho integrations read response.data, and HubSpot reads accessToken and expiresIn directly from a decoded SDK object. A native Response has none of those properties, regardless of its JSON body, so enabling syncing makes these refreshes throw or store invalid tokens. Decode and adapt the sync response for these callers, or change them to consume a consistent response contract.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem. In the sync path the code returns the fetch Response, while callers like Google (res.data) and HubSpot (token fields) expect integration-specific objects, which causes runtime errors.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Normalize sync responses to the contracts expected by SDK callers

The sync branch returns a native fetch Response, but several callers still expect the result of their original refresh function: Google and both Zoho integrations read response.data, and HubSpot reads accessToken and expiresIn directly from a decoded SDK object. A native Response has none of those properties, regardless of its JSON body, so enabling syncing makes these refreshes throw or store invalid tokens. Decode and adapt the sync response for these callers, or change them to consume a consistent response contract.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say the sync path returns a native fetch Response, while callers expect .data or SDK fields. This mismatch causes runtime failures, and both call for a consistent return shape.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Pass the Bigin credential owner's user ID to the sync endpoint

The third argument to refreshOAuthTokens is a Cal.com user ID, but this call passes credentialId. Consequently the external endpoint receives a credential table primary key as calcomUserId instead of the owner's ID. Since those IDs are unrelated, it can fail to find the account or return another user's credentials when the numbers coincide. Carry credential.userId through the refresh method and pass that value; team credentials should retain the null-user fallback.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: refreshOAuthTokens is passed credentialId where it should receive userId, which causes the sync to look up the wrong user.

false_positives.candidate:
Import Prisma before using it in Salesforce refresh

The new refresh path calls prisma.credential.update, but this module does not import or declare prisma. This fails TypeScript checking and, if transpiled without checking, throws ReferenceError on every Salesforce client initialization. Import the Prisma client used by the other integration services.

Send the Zoom app slug rather than its integration directory name

The refresh request sends appSlug: "zoomvideo", but Zoom credentials are registered with appId "zoom" and the OAuth callback also uses the slug "zoom". An external app store routing refreshes by the supplied appSlug cannot match this request to the Zoom app, preventing refreshes for synced Zoom credentials. Send "zoom" consistently.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Await reminder cancellations before completing the request

The cancellation helpers now perform the database deletion or cancelled-flag update, but their promises are discarded inside forEach and are not included in the awaited promises below. Previously the database reminder deletions were explicitly awaited. The handler can therefore return success before cancellation is persisted; in a serverless deployment, execution can stop after the response, leaving reminders active for a cancelled booking. Collect and await these helper promises, including the equivalent request-reschedule and workflow-update call sites.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem: the reminder deletion helpers are async but called inside forEach without await, so cancellations may not complete and reminders can stay active. Both cover the cancellation, reschedule, and workflow update call sites.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancel imminent reminders immediately instead of waiting for cron

Scheduled emails are now only marked cancelled, even when their send time is before the next 15-minute cron run. For example, cancelling a booking five minutes before its reminder is due leaves the email scheduled in SendGrid until after it is sent. The cron also deletes past-due reminder rows before processing cancellations, so it cannot recover this case. Reminders close to their send time need immediate provider cancellation.

Keep immediate cancellations recoverable when SendGrid rejects them

The immediateDelete path still submits cancellations arbitrarily far ahead of the send date, which consumes the same 100 pending-cancellation slots described in this PR. handleNewBooking uses this path for every reschedule. If SendGrid rejects a cancellation because that limit is reached, the error is swallowed and the reminder is never marked cancelled, so cron will not retry it and the old booking's email will still be sent. Workflow and step deletion also use this path and then cascade-delete the reminder rows, losing any retry opportunity.

Persist successful cancellations before another request can fail

The Prisma delete promises accumulated in the loop are lazy and execute only at Promise.all after every SendGrid cancellation succeeds. If any provider request fails, control jumps to the outer catch and none of the earlier successfully cancelled reminders are deleted. On subsequent runs those batches are submitted again; an already-cancelled batch can itself be rejected by SendGrid, repeatedly aborting processing before later reminders are reached. Handle failures per reminder and persist each successful cancellation independently so one failed batch cannot block all remaining cancellations.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

true_positives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

View-only group permission allows top-level group creation

canManage() accepts either the VIEW or MANAGE scope on all groups. GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() calls requireManage(), which delegates to this method, so an administrator granted only read access can create groups or move an existing subgroup to the top level. Require MANAGE alone here and add a test that an all-groups VIEW permission cannot perform these mutations.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorization resource IDs are used as group model IDs

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission() and returns it as a group ID. Authorization resources are created with generated IDs; the corresponding GroupModel ID is stored in the resource name by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource(). Consequently the permission lookup misses the specific resource and falls back to all-groups permissions, and the returned IDs cannot match user group memberships when UsersResource applies the search filter. Use the mapped group model ID rather than the authorization resource ID, and handle the all-groups resource separately.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission: it uses authorization resource IDs (groupResource.getId()) rather than the underlying group model IDs stored as resource names, causing permission checks to miss specific groups and fall back to all-groups, and returned IDs not to match group membership filters.

false_positives.candidate:
Individual group resources are not assigned the Groups type

When creating an individual group authorization resource, getOrCreateResource() sets its name and scopes but never sets its type to Groups. The new GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() discovers resources exclusively through findByType(..., "Groups", ...), so individual group permissions are omitted from that discovery. This prevents group-member permissions from supplying the group filters needed by user searches and counts. Assign the resource type when creating the resource and test discovery of an individual group's member-view permission.

Reject concatenated signatures with an unexpected length

concatenatedRSToASN1DER copies only the first signLength bytes without checking signature.length. An otherwise valid JOSE ECDSA signature with arbitrary bytes appended therefore produces exactly the same DER signature and can still verify successfully. JOSE requires the exact fixed signature length; accepting these inputs permits token/signature malleability. Check the input length and throw IOException before copying (also avoiding unchecked array-copy exceptions for short inputs).

Exercise the actual ES384 and ES512 curves and verify the reconstructed signature

All three tests generate an EC key using the provider's default curve (normally P-256), including testES384 and testES512. Changing the hash algorithm does not change the curve, so these tests only pad P-256 integers to larger lengths and never exercise real P-384 or P-521 signatures, including the long-form DER sequence length needed for P-521. Moreover, comparing two concatenated conversions can pass when the first conversion loses data. Generate the appropriate curve for each algorithm and verify the reconstructed DER signature against the original data and public key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Spawned workers do not pass the multiprocessing.Process type check

Workers are created with multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process, which creates SpawnProcess instances. These are not instances of the top-level multiprocessing.Process class, so this check skips kill() for every production worker. When a worker hangs, the manager starts a replacement without stopping the original; the original can subsequently resume flushing the same shards, causing concurrent processing and duplicate production. The identical check in join() also skips termination. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or explicitly distinguish threads from the spawn-context process type.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that spawn-context workers are SpawnProcess instances and therefore fail the multiprocessing.Process isinstance check, preventing hung workers from being killed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Terminate all remaining workers when the join deadline expires

When the shared join deadline expires, this loop breaks before stopping the current worker or any subsequent workers. This also happens if next_step.join(timeout) consumes the entire timeout. A worker blocked in Redis or Kafka therefore remains alive after the strategy is discarded during rebalancing, and may later resume flushing shards now owned by another consumer. false_positives.candidate:
Notification preferences are mutated by an unprotected GET request

The new GET unsubscribe route immediately saves notification preferences for the session's current user, without a recipient token or a POST confirmation. Rails CSRF protection does not protect GET requests, so another site can navigate a logged-in user to this URL and silently downgrade or mute notifications for a topic. Keep GET read-only and perform the change through a CSRF-protected request (or an appropriately validated recipient-specific unsubscribe token).

Direct save allows automatic tracking to undo unsubscribe

The unsubscribe action updates notification_level directly and saves the TopicUser without setting notifications_reason_id. For users whose topic tracking was automatic and whose reason is still nil, TopicUser.update_last_read explicitly restores tracking once the reading-time threshold is exceeded. Consequently, reading the topic after unsubscribing can undo this explicit preference. Use TopicUser.change, as set_notifications does, so the user_changed reason and notification-change metadata are recorded.

Client-side entry never performs the unsubscribe operation

The Ember unsubscribe route only loads the ordinary topic view through PostStream.loadTopicView; it never calls the unsubscribe endpoint or changes the notification level. When this URL is entered through client-side navigation, the Rails HTML GET action does not run, yet the template tells the user they will stop receiving notifications. Ensure this flow explicitly performs the preference change rather than relying on an initial full-page server request.

false_positives.candidate:
Date overrides bypass calendar and booking conflict checks

When an override exists on the slot's date, checkIfIsAvailable returns true before evaluating busy times. An override defines working availability, not permission to ignore existing bookings or external calendar events. Consequently, personal events and fixed or round-robin hosts with an override can expose slots that overlap their existing bookings. Continue to the busy-time checks after validating the override.

Override validation checks overlap instead of full slot containment

The new override checks reject only slots ending at or before the override start or starting after its end. For a fixed host available from 10:00 to 11:00, a round-robin slot from 09:30 to 10:30 or 10:30 to 11:30 therefore passes, even though the host is unavailable for part of the meeting. A slot starting exactly at 11:00 also passes. Require the entire slot to fit within an override interval.

Multiple override intervals reject slots inside a valid interval

dateOverrides.find searches for any interval that excludes the slot, rather than an interval that contains it. If a host has overrides of 09:00–12:00 and 14:00–17:00 on the same date, a 10:00 slot is rejected by the afternoon interval and a 15:00 slot by the morning interval. Split date-override availability can therefore lose all its slots. Group overrides by date and accept containment in any of that date's intervals.

Working-hours validation rejects ordinary split schedules

The workingHours.find predicate rejects a slot if it is outside any working-hours interval on that weekday. For a normal schedule of 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, morning slots fail against the afternoon interval and afternoon slots fail against the morning interval. Because every host now goes through this check, this removes valid slots even on dates without overrides. Validate that the full slot is contained in at least one applicable interval instead.

Timezone conversion discards midnight rollover

The converted override boundaries retain only hour and minute, discarding their date. For example, a UTC override from 22:00 to 23:00 viewed in UTC+01:30 becomes startTime 1410 and endTime 30. buildSlots discards that range because start is greater than end, so the valid 23:30–00:30 availability disappears. Converted overrides that cross an attendee's midnight need to be split across the corresponding attendee dates rather than reduced to a single minute-of-day range.

Every import() in this object executes as soon as the app-store index is loaded, so accessing a single calendar or payment provider still starts loading and evaluating all app packages. This splits the modules into chunks but does not defer unused apps, retaining the all-app initialization cost on cold starts. Store loader functions instead and invoke only the selected loader at the call sites. This also allows import failures to be handled by the requesting caller rather than leaving rejected promises for unused apps unobserved.

The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
